title: The Summer of 1787
objective: After this level you can explain how the Great Compromise settled the fight between large and small states at the Constitutional Convention.
summary: At the Constitutional Convention of 1787, big states wanted representation by population and small states wanted equal votes. The Great Compromise gave them both, by one vote.

cards.headline: In July 1787, the Constitution nearly died over one question.
cards.body: Should a big state count for more than a small one? The answer passed by a single vote.

cards.headline: A summer in Philadelphia
cards.body: From May 25 to September 17, 1787, delegates met at the Pennsylvania State House in Philadelphia. 55 took part; Rhode Island sent no one. They elected George Washington to preside. Remember Level 31: they had come to fix a government whose Congress could only ask the states for money.

cards.headline: Big states, small states
cards.body: Virginia’s plan, offered by Edmund Randolph, called for a two-house Congress with each state represented by its population or wealth. That suited big states. William Paterson’s New Jersey Plan answered with equal representation for every state, which suited small ones. Under the Articles, each state had one vote, and small states weren’t eager to give that up.

cards.headline: Split the difference
cards.body: Connecticut’s Roger Sherman and Oliver Ellsworth gave their name to the fix: seats in the House by population, and equal seats for every state in the Senate. The convention adopted this Great Compromise on July 16, 1787, by one vote. Every time you hear that each state has two senators, you’re hearing the echo of that summer.

cards.headline: The Summer of 1787: explained
learned: The convention met in Philadelphia, May to September 1787
Virginia Plan: by population; New Jersey Plan: equal states
Great Compromise: House by population, Senate equal

questions.prompt: At the Constitutional Convention, what did the New Jersey Plan propose?

options.label: Seats based on population or wealth
Keeping the Articles with no changes
options.rationale: It proposed a new Congress with equal representation.

options.label: A Congress chosen by Rhode Island’s rules

questions.explanation: William Paterson’s New Jersey Plan gave every state equal representation.

questions.prompt: How did the Great Compromise settle the fight between large and small states?

options.label: Senate seats by population, equal House seats
One house where each state had one vote
House seats by population, equal Senate seats
Large states got two votes, small states one
options.rationale: Representation was split between two houses instead.

questions.explanation: The House follows population; the Senate gives every state equal seats.

questions.prompt: The part of the new Congress that kept the Articles’ idea that every state counts equally was _____.

options.label: both houses equally
options.rationale: Only one house gives every state equal seats.

questions.explanation: The Senate gives every state equal seats, as the Articles gave every state one vote.
